headline: Man saved from rubble after eight days

sources.title: Man pulled from rubble in 'miraculous' rescue 8 days after Venezuela earthquakes - CNN
'Miracle': Trapped man rescued eight days after Venezuela earthquakes - Al Jazeera
Venezuelan security guard pulled alive from earthquake rubble after 8 days - PBS News

chunks.text: Eight days after two [[powerful]] earthquakes hit Venezuela, [[rescuers]] have {{pulled a man out}} of a [[collapsed]] building, and he is still alive. The man, a security guard named Hernan Gil, was [[trapped]] when a shopping mall parking lot {{came down}} [[on top of]] him in the coastal town of La Guaira. Doctors say he is now in good condition. Many people are calling the rescue a [[miracle]].

verbs.wrong: To help someone walk out of a dangerous place
verbs.correct: To remove someone from a dangerous place

chunks.text: When the building fell, Gil {{ended up}} trapped inside a small concrete booth in the basement. Experts say the strong booth {{held up}} and formed a protective pocket that shielded him from the falling [[debris]]. For eight long days, he {{held on}} under tons of [[rubble]], with no food and very little water.

verbs.wrong: To hide somewhere to stay safe
verbs.correct: To finally be in a particular situation

verbs.wrong: To keep something safe inside it
verbs.correct: To stay strong and not fall or fail

verbs.wrong: To stay calm and quiet in danger
verbs.correct: To survive or continue in a hard situation

chunks.text: Rescue teams from seven countries {{teamed up}} to save him. According to Chile's fire brigade, it took more than 70 hours of [[careful]] work to {{dig out}} the security booth. The workers [[refused]] to {{give up}}, [[even though]] [[the best chance]] of finding [[survivors]] usually ends after about three days. In the end, their effort {{paid off}}.

verbs.wrong: To arrive at the same time
verbs.correct: To join together to work with others

verbs.wrong: To break a hole in something hard
verbs.correct: To remove someone or something by digging
To bring a good result after effort

chunks.text: At the hospital, doctors say Gil is slowly {{getting over}} his [[terrible]] [[ordeal]]. The twin earthquakes have {{turned out}} to be [[among the worst]] in Venezuela's history, killing more than 2,500 people. Thousands of families still do not know what happened to their [[missing]] relatives. For a country [[full of]] sadness, this one rescue has {{brought about}} a [[rare]] moment of hope.

verbs.wrong: To try to forget something bad that happened
To be reported in the news many times
verbs.correct: To end up being a certain way

verbs.wrong: To remind people of something good

tf.s: For eight long days, the security guard held up under tons of rubble with almost no food or water.
tf.why: The man held on (survived in a hard situation) for eight days. Hold up means to stay strong and not fall, which describes the booth, not a person.

tf.s: In the end, the rescuers' effort paid off and they saved the man alive.
tf.why: The workers refused to give up, and in the end their effort paid off (brought a good result).

tf.s: After more than 70 hours of digging, the tired rescue teams gave up, and the man was found alive.
tf.why: The rescue workers refused to give up. After more than 70 hours their effort paid off and they dug the man out alive.

tf.s: Rescue teams from seven countries teamed up to save the trapped man.
tf.why: Rescue teams from seven countries teamed up (joined together) to save him.

tf.s: Doctors say Gil is slowly getting over his terrible ordeal.
tf.why: At the hospital, doctors say he is slowly getting over (recovering from) the ordeal and is now in good condition.

tf.s: Gil brought about his own terrible ordeal under the rubble.
tf.why: Gil did not cause what happened to him. Bring about means to cause something to happen, but it was the earthquake that trapped him. Doctors say he is getting over the ordeal.
